extracted.intended_audience: researchers, science policy analysts, and funders interested in grant peer review behavior and rubric design
extracted.subtask_description: Linguistic analysis of grant peer review reports to identify which words, rhetorical patterns, and topics predict reviewer scores and to surface implicit criteria used in funding decisions. Useful for researchers studying peer review, and for funders designing or auditing review rubrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive evaluation words
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of explicitly positive evaluative words is correlated with higher applicant scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'excellent', 'innovative', 'outstanding'. Use of such words signals enthusiasm and tends to predict favorable scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superlatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of superlative language is a positive predictor of applicant score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'best', 'most original'. Superlatives indicate strong endorsement and associate with higher scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmation language
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirming phrasing (clear, positive assertions) correlates with higher scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmation language signals reviewer agreement/confidence; absence or replacement by hedging reduces score likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of negation (negative polarity) correlates with lower applicant scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'not', 'no', 'never'. Negations often highlight problems or disconfirmations and are associated with negative evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative evaluation words
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly negative evaluative terms correlate with lower scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'weak', 'unclear', 'insufficient'. These words directly flag perceived deficiencies and predict worse outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion words / caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of exclusionary or contrastive connectives correlates with lower scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'but', 'however', 'except'. Such words introduce caveats that temper praise and often indicate reservations leading to lower scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative language / hedging
rubrics_metrics.description: Tentative or hedging language correlates with lower applicant scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'maybe', 'possibly'. Hedging signals uncertainty or disagreement among reviewers and is predictive of lower formal scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research project descriptive words (long descriptive discussion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater use of descriptive project language in reviews was unexpectedly correlated NEGATIVELY with scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive description often occurs when reviewers are debating problems; long descriptive passages can be a signal of contention rather than endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track record discussion length
rubrics_metrics.description: More text devoted to applicants' CV/track record correlated NEGATIVELY with scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long track-record discussions frequently reflect concerns; simply increasing attention to CV details is not a positive indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological rigor emerges as a primary implicit reviewer criterion and is the most-discussed weakness category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews frequently scrutinize methods; methodological problems are a common basis for negative evaluation and rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical framing / novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical framing and novelty operate as a core implicit strength criterion and were the most-discussed strength category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, novel theoretical contribution is rewarded in text and scoring; reviewers highlight originality as a positive factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track record sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficiency of the applicant's track record is an implicit criterion and a frequent marginal concern in reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track record is discussed often but more attention to it can signal doubts; explicit positive statements about an adequate record help but detailed debate may hurt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility of work plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Feasibility (practicality and realism of the proposed plan) is an implicit reviewer criterion affecting scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise, convincing work plans reduce discussion length and lower perceived risk; doubts about feasibility trigger negative language and lower scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance / contribution to field
rubrics_metrics.description: Perceived significance or expected contribution is an implicit criterion that informs positive assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear statements of contribution and impact are associated with positive evaluative language and higher scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel focus on weakest proposals (elimination focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panels tend to concentrate on identifying weakest proposals to reject rather than on identifying the strongest to fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This behavioral pattern implies that rubrics and processes emphasizing elimination may exacerbate conservative outcomes; attention tends to concentrate where there are problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-risk proposals provoke longer discussions
rubrics_metrics.description: Risky or controversial proposals trigger longer panel discussions, and longer discussions are correlated with lower scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer discussion length is often a signal of perceived risk; panels' deliberation dynamics can therefore disadvantage high-risk/high-reward proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hedging as signal of reviewer disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers use hedging and tentative language to signal disagreement, and that signaling converts into lower formal scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detecting hedging in review text can reveal hidden dissent that impacts scoring; hedges are diagnostic of eventual negative outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative scoring equilibrium
rubrics_metrics.description: When panels fail to reach enthusiasm consensus, conservative (safe) scoring becomes the equilibrium outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In absence of strong positive agreement, panels default to risk-averse decisions; rubrics that rely on consensus can therefore favor conservative projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion length as an implicit score signal
rubrics_metrics.description: Length of review/discussion itself functions as a score signal: longer reviews typically indicate more contention and lower outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring discussion length can serve as an audit signal; designers should be aware that length correlates with negative scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decouple discussion amount from score to fund riskier work
rubrics_metrics.description: To fund risky, high-reward work, rubric designers should avoid letting amount of discussion automatically translate into lower scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: create rubric elements or procedures that prevent long deliberations about risk from being treated as de facto negative judgments (e.g., explicit 'risk-reward' dimensions, separate scoring for novelty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic auditing to surface implicit criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzing past review texts linguistically can surface implicit criteria and signals that are not captured in formal rubrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use LIWC-style or similar textual analyses to reveal what reviewers actually reward/punish; use findings to revise rubrics to better align formal criteria with actual decision drivers.
